title: Tonkatsu
subtitle: Japanese breaded pork cutlet
excerpt: Tonkatsu is a thick pork cutlet coated in panko breadcrumbs and shallow-fried until deeply golden. The crust stays crisp while the meat inside remains juicy, and the whole thing comes together in under 30 minutes.
sourceNotes: Tonkatsu was introduced to Japan in the Meiji era, adapted from European cutlet techniques. It is now one of Japan's most popular comfort foods, typically served with shredded cabbage and tonkatsu sauce.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bread the pork up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate uncovered. Fry just before serving.

content.text: Tonkatsu relies on panko breadcrumbs for its signature shatter. Unlike fine dried breadcrumbs, panko is coarse and open-textured, which means it fries up with far more surface area and far more crunch. The pork cutlet underneath stays moist because the frying is quick: once the crust is deep golden, the meat is done.

Tonkatsu sauce is the classic accompaniment: mix 2 tablespoons of Worcestershire sauce with 1 tablespoon of ketchup and a teaspoon of soy sauce as a quick version. Serve alongside a mound of very finely shredded raw cabbage, which cuts through the richness of the fried crust.

Lay the pork cutlets on a board. Using a sharp knife, score the fat and connective tissue around the edge of each cutlet at 2 cm intervals. This prevents the cutlet from curling as it fries. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set up three shallow dishes: one with the flour, one with the beaten egg, and one with the panko. Dust each cutlet in flour and shake off any excess, then dip it in the egg, letting the surplus drip off. Press both sides firmly into the panko so the crumbs adhere in an even layer.
Pour the oil into a large frying pan to a depth of about 1 cm. Heat over a medium-high hob until a pinch of panko dropped in sizzles immediately. The oil should be around 170 to 180C.

Lower the cutlets into the oil carefully. Fry for 4 to 5 minutes on the first side without moving them, until the crust is deep golden. Flip and fry for another 3 to 4 minutes. If using a probe thermometer, the centre of the pork should read 68C.
Transfer to a wire rack or a plate lined with kitchen paper. Leave to rest for 2 minutes before slicing into thick strips. Serve immediately with the shredded cabbage and tonkatsu sauce on the side.

items.symptom: The crust falls off during frying
items.cause: The flour base was too thick or the egg did not coat evenly, so the panko had nothing to grip.
items.fix: Shake off excess flour before dipping in egg, and press the panko on firmly. Refrigerating the breaded cutlets for 30 minutes before frying also helps the coating set.

items.symptom: The crust is golden but the pork is still pink inside
items.cause: The oil was too hot, so the crust coloured before the meat had time to cook through.
items.fix: Reduce the heat to medium. If the crust is already done, transfer the cutlets to a baking tray and finish in a 180C oven for 5 to 8 minutes.

items.symptom: The crust is pale and greasy
items.cause: The oil was not hot enough when the cutlets went in, so the panko absorbed oil rather than crisping quickly.
items.fix: Always test the oil with a pinch of panko before adding the cutlets. The crumbs should sizzle briskly within 2 seconds of contact.

items.symptom: The cutlet curls up in the pan
items.cause: The connective tissue around the edge was not scored, causing it to tighten as it heats.
items.fix: Score the edge before breading. If it has already curled, press it flat gently with a spatula for the first minute of frying.
